cards.title: Automate Instagram media to Google Business Profile
cards.summary: Trigger a no-code workflow so every Instagram business post is auto-published as Google Business Profile media, building local SEO signals without manual uploads.
cards.use_when: You manage a local store with an Instagram business account and a Google Business Profile, and want to keep local listings fresh without manually re-uploading images or videos.
steps: Confirm you have admin access to the Google Business Profile and an Instagram business account linked to the same brand — these are non-negotiable prerequisites.
In Pabbly (or Make/Zapier), create a folder named after the client/store, then create a workflow named e.g. 'Instagram to Google Business'.
Set the trigger app to Instagram, trigger event 'new media updated to the account', and authenticate the Instagram business connection.
Add an action: Google Business Profile > upload media/photo (choose image or video to match the source). Authenticate the Google account and select the target location.
For the media URL field, map the 'media URL' attribute pulled from the Instagram post in the trigger test data. Optionally set a category.
Save and send a test. Verify on the Google Business Profile photos/videos tab that the asset appears, then toggle the workflow ON for autopilot.
caveats: Automation tool interfaces and field names change — verify the current UI before building.
Pabbly free tier may be sufficient for a single store; scaling many locations likely needs a paid plan.
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx

cards.title: Auto-convert blog posts into Google Business posts via RSS
cards.summary: Use an RSS-feed trigger plus an internet-enabled LLM to rewrite each new blog post into a sub-1,500-character Google Business post with a CTA link.
cards.use_when: You publish blog content and want an automated, ongoing stream of Google Business posts driving traffic back to those articles without manual rewriting.
steps: Create a workflow triggered by an RSS feed ('new item in feed'). For most WordPress sites the feed URL is yoursite.com/feed — for other platforms, look up or generate a feed.
Add an Open Router 'chat completion' action and connect it using your API key.
Select a model with native internet access (e.g. Perplexity Sonar) so it can read the post URL directly instead of needing a separate scraper.

Set role to 'user' and paste a prompt instructing the model to visit the blog URL, read it, and rewrite it in the same tone of voice but under ~1,450–1,500 characters to fit Google Business limits. Map the RSS feed's URL field into the prompt.
Ask for a call-to-action line and, optionally, suppress hashtags if you don't want them.
Add a Google Business Profile action: create an action post. Map the message content to the model output, set action type to 'Learn more', and map the button URL to the blog post URL.
Test, confirm the post appears on the profile, then enable the workflow.
caveats: The presenter could not explain why Open Router requires a sitemap/website field — treat it as a setup quirk to just satisfy.
Verify current character limits and field names; they may differ from the tutorial.
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx

cards.title: Auto-respond to positive Google reviews, gate negative ones
cards.summary: Filter reviews by star rating and let an LLM draft and post replies only to positive reviews, keeping negative ones for human handling.
cards.use_when: You want to maintain fast, consistent responses to positive local reviews at scale while keeping full human control over reputation-sensitive negative feedback.
steps: Create a workflow triggered by Google Business Profile 'new review'. Authenticate and select the location.
Add a filter node using the star-rating label. The tutorial filters to star rating greater than 4 so only clearly positive reviews proceed automatically.
Add an Open Router chat-completion action using a cheap model (e.g. GPT-5 Mini). Free models work but hit rate/usage limits under volume.

Paste a review-responder prompt that includes: business type/context, instructions for the positive case, and fallback instructions if a below-threshold review slips through (thank, apologize, state one proactive step, give contact email/phone).
Map the review comment and star rating into the prompt, set role to 'user', and generate the reply. Consider routing the draft to a Google Sheet for human review before publishing.

Add a Google Business Profile 'create a reply' action (not the legacy version), map the account, and map the reply field to the model output; the latest review is picked automatically. Test and enable.
caveats: The presenter advises replying with AI only to positive reviews — negative reviews need a human touch to avoid errors.
If filtering is used, the negative-review fallback prompt may never run; decide deliberately whether to keep the filter or let all reviews generate drafts for review.
Verify current action names in the automation tool and Google Business Profile.

cards.title: Choose an automation platform by skill and scale
cards.summary: Match the no-code/self-host automation tool to your coding comfort and volume: Pabbly for lowest friction, Make for flexibility, n8n for scale and cost savings.
cards.use_when: You are deciding which automation tool to run your store's SEO/marketing workflows on, weighing ease of setup against cost and flexibility.
steps: For lowest friction with no coding at all, use Pabbly — plug-and-play for straightforward Instagram-to-GBP or RSS-to-post workflows.
For flexibility and broadest app integrations via click-and-drag, use Make; the presenter uses it most but notes slightly more complexity than Pabbly.
For self-hosting and saving on subscription costs, use n8n — open-source, requires some coding comfort, and suited to offering automation services at scale.
Directory-check current pricing and integration coverage before committing; free tiers may cover single-store setups but not multi-location scale.
Reuse one automation platform across all your SEO workflows (media upload, blog repurposing, review replies) so connections and credentials stay consolidated.
caveats: Tool pricing, free-tier limits and integration lists change frequently — verify before choosing.
Self-hosting n8n shifts maintenance and uptime responsibility to you.

cards.title: Use one Open Router key to test and route LLM models
cards.summary: Adopt a single Open Router API key to access many LLMs, test model quality on a simple prompt, and route cheap models for high-volume automations.
cards.use_when: You need to pick and pay for LLMs for store automations (content rewriting, review replies) without managing multiple provider accounts or API keys.
steps: Create an Open Router account and use the chat/side-by-side feature to send the same prompt to multiple flagship models (e.g. Gemini, Claude Sonnet, Grok, GPT) and compare outputs before committing.
Add credits — the presenter tops up only $5, which 'goes a very long way' with cheap models; avoid auto-top-up unless needed.
Create a dedicated API key per use case (e.g. 'family automation') so you can track credit spending by workflow.
Copy and securely save the key immediately — it is shown only once.

In your automation tool, connect Open Router using that key, and select a model matched to the task: an internet-enabled model (Perplexity Sonar) for reading/rewriting pages, and a cheap model (e.g. GPT-5 Mini) for simple review replies.
caveats: Model names, availability and pricing change frequently — verify current options and costs.
Free/open-source models have usage limits that can block you at volume.
Never share or expose your API key; rotate if leaked.

cards.title: Don't automate SEO before the fundamentals work
cards.summary: Resist automating everything at scale until your core SEO is sound, because premature automation causes costly 'horror case' failures.
cards.use_when: You are tempted to automate listing posts, review replies or content repurposing before your store's SEO basics (site structure, content quality, local profile setup) are in good shape.
steps: Before wiring up any workflow, confirm the fundamentals the workflow depends on: a properly configured Google Business Profile, a working RSS/blog structure, and clean site data.
Prioritize automations that reinforce fundamentals (consistent local media, repurposed content, timely review replies) rather than ones that paper over gaps.
Roll out one workflow at a time and verify the output manually (e.g. check the GBP tab, inspect the generated post/reply) before enabling autopilot.
For anything that affects published, reputation-facing content (posts, review replies), keep a human review or draft step.
When output quality degrades even with good inputs, fix the underlying content/data rather than buying more automation or models.
caveats: The presenter frames this as a warning from observed failures, not a strict rule with measured benchmarks.
Some low-risk, reversible automations (e.g. media upload) may be safely enabled earlier.

cards.title: Skip heavy dashboards: GSC + GA into an LLM for decisions
cards.summary: Use Google Search Console and Google Analytics data fed to an LLM instead of building elaborate reports, so you still make data-driven decisions quickly.
cards.use_when: You need recurring store SEO decisions (which pages/queries/locations to prioritize) but lack time or budget for polished reporting dashboards.
steps: Ensure Google Search Console and Google Analytics are installed and collecting data — this is the essential baseline.
Pull the relevant data (queries, pages, locations, trends) from GSC and GA.
Feed that data into an LLM (the presenter references a custom GPT) and ask specific decision questions, e.g. which pages to refresh or where to push local content.
Act on the LLM's suggestions as hypotheses, then validate against GSC/GA movement after changes.
Repeat on a cadence instead of maintaining static reports.
caveats: The presenter explicitly says to 'not complicate analytics' — this trades report polish for speed, so verify LLM-derived conclusions against raw GSC/GA numbers.
Custom-GPT links and interfaces change; verify current setup.
